title: The Athenaeum — Weekly Sittings
subtitle: Drawn from the week's Discourse Reports, Monday Nov 16 to Sunday Nov 22, 2026: the week's top stories, merged where they ran on several nights, each put to a table of historical thinkers.

integrity.quotation_policy: Quotation marks appear only around verbatim public-domain text matched against a fetched source; everything else is paraphrase.

briefing.question: Is peace secured by great powers dividing the world among themselves, or does a just order require that small nations have a voice in their own fate?
briefing.agreed: Talking beats fighting; the strong cannot settle what the weak are owed.
briefing.split: Kant forbids trading states; Machiavelli trusts no one; Augustine asks for justice.

briefing.question: Who decides when a nation goes to war, and how far may a legislature go to stop one it never authorized: is withholding funds principled restraint or a dangerous gamble with the common good?
briefing.agreed: War needs proper authority, openly given.
briefing.split: Madison, a targeted funding bar; Hamilton, a clean vote; Aquinas, right intention.

briefing.question: Does a mandate end on election day or on the last day of a term? The legitimacy of lame-duck power, and how independent judges should be of the people who choose them.
briefing.agreed: The lame-duck Senate keeps its lawful power.
briefing.split: Hamilton, confirm with scrutiny; Brutus, term limits; Locke, heed voters; Burke, norms.

briefing.question: Does art that depicts vice teach vice, or let us see it clearly? What we love shapes who we become.
briefing.agreed: Protect children; ask what play does to the player.
briefing.split: Plato, we become what we imitate; Aristotle, catharsis; Mill, adults are free.

briefing.question: Once a court has spoken, does a convicted person keep the right to publicly deny guilt, and do victims have a right not to hear it? And before a court has spoken, how far may the community judge?
briefing.agreed: No guilt before trial; victims first after it.
briefing.split: Blackstone and Beccaria, enforce prison rules; Mill, defend speech; Aristotle, judge the message.

briefing.question: Should a society protect what people hold sacred from mockery, or is the freedom to offend part of what lets faith and art both stay alive?
briefing.agreed: No law against the show; the petition is speech.
briefing.split: Aquinas, derision can wrong; Milton and Tertullian, answer it; Locke, charity.

briefing.question: What does solidarity with one's own people demand, and how does it coexist with universal love of neighbor? Can a pluralist, equal citizenship be built where faith communities have long feared one another?
briefing.agreed: Equal citizenship; love of one's own need not exclude the neighbor.
briefing.split: Tertullian, a natural right; Augustine, one Church of many peoples; Washington, equal immunities.

briefing.question: What is the proper relation between the City of God and the City of Man: should faith shape the laws, or stay free of the state?
briefing.agreed: Believers may serve the city; no forced faith.
briefing.split: Calvin and Leo, rulers support faith; Williams and Madison, a civil state; Augustine, no holy nation.

briefing.question: Is human mastery of nature a gift to be used or a power to be restrained, and who sets the limits? What is the human person for, and should machines do what makes us human?
briefing.agreed: Technology should serve persons, not master them.
briefing.split: Bacon, discovery relieves; Leo XIII, protect workers; Kant, keep a responsible person.

short_edition.why: Picked by prominence across the week and balance across sections: the Trump, Xi and Putin summit and its Yalta image, which ran on five of seven nights; Sunday's lead story on Democrats weighing the Dec. 11 funding deadline to end the Iran war; the record launch of Grand Theft Auto VI, which ran on three nights; and the week's running argument over faith and the state, from Christian nationalism's two kingdoms debate to Moscow as the Third Rome.

sittings.headline: Trump posts The Great Powers 1945, 2026, pairing himself, Xi and Putin with Yalta's Big Three
sittings.question: Is peace secured by great powers dividing the world among themselves, or does a just order require that small nations have a voice in their own fate?

setup.text: The week's longest-running story, reported on five of seven nights (Nov 16, 18, 19, 20 and 22). Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin held the first formal three-way leaders' meeting in Shenzhen on the sidelines of APEC and signed a four-point Declaration toward Peace calling for UN reform, more refined-petroleum production, a dialogue on nuclear risks, and a statement that the International Criminal Court must not abuse its jurisdiction, with no clear breakthrough on Ukraine or Iran. Two days later Trump posted an image setting a photo of the three beside Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin at Yalta, which drew alarm in Ukraine and Eastern Europe and praise from supporters as peace through strength.

sittings.why_these_chairs: Thucydides speaks first because the report names his Melian Dialogue, the oldest account of the strong dealing with the weak, and because his history is a study of how great powers drift into war. Kant follows because the report names Perpetual Peace, whose preliminary articles forbid trading one state to another and treating treaties as truces. Machiavelli is seated as the classic defender of dealing with rulers as they are, not as they ought to be. Grotius is seated because he founded the law of nations on a common human nature that binds great and small states alike, and he warned against noble pretexts. Augustine closes because his City of God asks what a kingdom is once justice is taken away, and because he insisted that all war is waged for the sake of some peace. Left off: Metternich and Castlereagh, whose Congress of Vienna the report cites, left no sustained philosophical writing on the question. The three leaders, Ukraine's President Zelenskyy and the American critics named in the reports are context only.

opening.text: This week's subject: is peace secured by great powers dividing the world among themselves, or does a just order require that small nations have a voice in their own fate? The report gives one side as supporters, who say peace among nuclear powers requires their leaders to talk directly; a summit of the three largest powers is realism, not betrayal, could prevent a larger war, and shows a president willing to deal with adversaries where predecessors only issued statements. Some also see the International Criminal Court as an unaccountable body that claims power over nations that never consented to it. The other side is critics, who say Yalta is remembered in Warsaw, Kyiv and the Baltics as the moment the West handed half of Europe to Soviet domination; celebrating it with Putin, whose army is still at war in Ukraine, signals that small nations' sovereignty is negotiable and blurs the line between free and unfree governments. Thucydides, the reports quote your Athenians. Begin.

chairs.name: Thucydides
works: History of the Peloponnesian War, Book I and Book V (the Melian Conference)

turn.text: I wrote down what the Athenian envoys told the Melians, and I did not soften it: “right, as the world goes, is only in question between equals in power, while the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must.” (History of the Peloponnesian War, Book V, ch. XVII (the Melian Conference)) Notice that I put those words in the mouths of men who were about to destroy a small island that only wished to stay neutral. I recorded them because powerful states say such things to themselves, not because I admired them. The Melians pleaded “that you should not destroy what is our common protection, the privilege of being allowed in danger to invoke what is fair and right” (History of the Peloponnesian War, Book V, ch. XVII (the Melian Conference)) They were right, and they died anyway.

turn.text: So I would tell the supporters that they are correct about one thing: great powers do settle much among themselves, and a meeting of the three strongest is better than a war among them. But I would tell them also what happened to Athens. A city that learns to speak only the language of strength teaches its rivals and its allies to speak it too, and when its own fortunes turned, no one remembered any claim of right on its behalf. A peace made over the heads of the small is a peace that rests entirely on the continued strength of the large.

chairs.name: Immanuel Kant
works: Perpetual Peace (1795), Section I, Preliminary Articles 1 and 2

turn.text: Thucydides describes how the world goes; I tried to describe how it must go if peace is to be more than an interval. My second preliminary article is plain: “No state having an independent existence--whether it be great or small--shall be acquired by another through inheritance, exchange, purchase or donation.” (Perpetual Peace, Section I, Preliminary Article 2) A state, I said, is not a possession. “It is a society of human beings over whom no one but itself has the right to rule and to dispose.” (Perpetual Peace, Section I, Preliminary Article 2) To treat it as an item that great powers may exchange at a table is to deny it the moral standing of a person.

I do not object to rulers meeting; I object to the idea that their meeting can dispose of a people who were not present. On my terms, the small nation's voice is not a courtesy. It is the condition under which any settlement can be a peace at all.

I wrote for princes in the world as it is, where a ruler who refuses to deal with his strongest rivals simply leaves the field to others. The supporters understand something I learned from the Romans: “war is not to be avoided, but is only to be put off to the advantage of others” (The Prince, ch. III) If a war can be headed off by sitting down with the other great powers, a prudent prince sits down.

chairs.name: Hugo Grotius
chairs.tradition: Natural law and the law of nations
works: The Rights of War and Peace (1625), Book II, ch. XXV

turn.text: Machiavelli is candid, and candor is useful. But I wrote my book because I had watched princes keep faith only while it served them, and I saw where that led. Nations are bound to one another by more than interest. “The last and most extensive motive is the common tie of one COMMON NATURE, which alone is sufficient to oblige men to assist each other.” (The Rights of War and Peace, Book II, ch. XXV, §VI) That tie does not loosen because a nation is small or far away. It is the ground on which a weaker people may appeal to the stronger, and the ground on which a court of nations can claim any authority at all.

chairs.name: Augustine
works: City of God (426), Book IV, ch. 4 and Book XIX, ch. 12

turn.text: Grotius speaks of pretexts; I asked what remains of a kingdom when the pretext is all that is left. “Justice being taken away, then, what are kingdoms but great robberies? For what are robberies themselves, but little kingdoms?” (City of God IV.4) I meant that the difference between an empire and a band of thieves is justice, not size. Great powers that divide the world without regard to what is owed to smaller peoples have not become more than kingdoms. They have become larger robberies.

I would only ask what kind of peace is being sought: the tranquillity of order, in which each is given his due, or a quiet imposed by the strong on those who were not asked.

sittings.headline: Democrats split over using the Dec. 11 funding deadline to force an end to the Iran war
sittings.question: Who decides when a nation goes to war, and how far may a legislature go to stop one it never authorized: is withholding funds principled restraint or a dangerous gamble with the common good?

sittings.why_these_chairs: Madison speaks first because the report names Federalist 51 and Article I's war and spending clauses, and because he wrote more than any founder on why the war power belongs to the legislature. Hamilton answers because the report names Federalist 70 on energy in the executive, the strongest founding case for presidential direction of foreign affairs. Locke is seated because his Second Treatise names the federative power of war and peace and asks how far it can be bound by standing law. Aquinas closes because the report names the just war tradition's requirement of right authority, which he set down as the first condition of a just war. opening.text: This week's subject: who decides when a nation goes to war, and how far may a legislature go to stop one it never authorized? turn.text: The purse was given to the House on purpose. I wrote in the fifty-eighth paper that “This power over the purse may, in fact, be regarded as the most complete and effectual weapon with which any constitution can arm the immediate representatives of the people, for obtaining a redress of every grievance, and for carrying into effect every just and salutary measure.” (Federalist No. 58) Every grievance includes the gravest one, a war the people's representatives never chose. Later, answering Hamilton in the Helvidius letters, I argued that the power to decide on war is legislative by nature, and that the executive, which conducts war, is the branch most tempted to begin one (Helvidius letters, paraphrased).

I told New York that the President's command “It would amount to nothing more than the supreme command and direction of the military and naval forces, as first General and admiral of the Confederacy; while that of the British king extends to the declaring of war and to the raising and regulating of fleets and armies--all which, by the Constitution under consideration, would appertain to the legislature.” (Federalist No. 69) I defended energy in the conduct of a war, not a power to begin one alone. The other side is critics, many of them religious, who say you become what you rehearse; hundreds of hours enacting cruelty for fun dull the conscience, and calling it satire does not change what the player is invited to delight in. Some pastors instead urge engaging gamers rather than dismissing them. By week's end the report added a second question, about officials using an adults-only game to sell policy and who is responsible for forming the young. Plato, you started this argument. Begin.

Mill leaves adults free and puts children in their parents' care.

sittings.why_these_chairs: Beccaria speaks first because his Of Crimes and Punishments is the founding text on why no one may be treated as guilty before sentence and why punishment must have a limited purpose. Blackstone answers because the report names his ratio, that it is better for ten guilty to escape than for one innocent to suffer. Mill is seated because the report names the free-speech argument that rights are tested by the least sympathetic speaker, and because he drew the line between social disapproval and social tyranny. Aristotle closes because his account of corrective justice explains what a court's sentence restores, and what it leaves to the community. Left off: Bonhoeffer, named on Nov 17, who is in copyright and whose writing on cheap grace concerns the church more than the courts. Brand, his wife, Manson, Walliams, the signatories and officials are context only; the sitting takes the court's verdict as the report states it and judges no pending case.

chairs.name: Cesare Beccaria
works: Of Crimes and Punishments (1764), chs. XII and XV

turn.text: I will begin with the cases where no court has spoken, because there my rule is absolute. “A man cannot be called guilty before sentence has been passed on him by a judge, nor can society deprive him of its protection till it has been decided that he has broken the condition on which it was granted.” (Of Crimes and Punishments, ch. XII) A petition to cancel a concert before a trial is not a sentence, and a promoter may make his own decisions. But a public that treats an accused man as already convicted has taken over the judge's office without the judge's duties of evidence and hearing.

XV) If the statement from prison torments the women who testified, prison rules may rightly forbid it, for preventing further injury to them is within the purpose of punishment. But punishment that reaches beyond its purpose becomes cruelty, and I would want the rule applied to what the statement does to the victims, not to the mere fact that a convicted man insists he is innocent.

sittings.headline: 126,000 sign a petition calling on Netflix to pull The Body as blasphemous
sittings.question: Should a society protect what people hold sacred from mockery, or is the freedom to offend part of what lets faith and art both stay alive?

setup.text: Reported on Nov 16 and Nov 19. A CitizenGo petition asking Netflix to cancel The Body, a coming-of-age horror series about Catholic school girls whose prophetic visions set off mass hysteria, grew from more than 90,000 to more than 126,000 signatures; the show drew 5.1 million views in its first five days, counter-petitions asked for a second season, and its creator said it was not meant to be hyper-critical of religion. The same week the reports carried other fights over speech and the sacred: a Karnataka order confiscating a book on Basavanna, renewed outcry over a Pakistani Christian mother on death row for blasphemy, and a viral clip of a priest insulting Muhammad.

sittings.headline: Pope Leo XIV warns of an exodus of Middle East Christians as Syrian patriarchs condemn kidnappings and torture
sittings.question: What does solidarity with one's own people demand, and how does it coexist with universal love of neighbor? Can a pluralist, equal citizenship be built where faith communities have long feared one another?

setup.text: Reported on Nov 17 and Nov 20. Syria's Greek Orthodox, Syriac Orthodox and Melkite Greek Catholic patriarchs jointly condemned kidnappings, ransom demands and assaults targeting Christians, including an attack on the Melkite Archbishop of Homs, and urged authorities to investigate and guarantee equal citizenship. On Nov 20 Pope Leo XIV told the Catholic Near East Welfare Association that war, persecution, instability and poverty are driving Eastern Christians from their homelands, and called helping families stay an essential work of hope.

sittings.why_these_chairs: Tertullian speaks first because the report names his line on the blood of martyrs, and because his letter To Scapula is the earliest Christian argument that worship is a natural right owed to everyone. Augustine follows because the City of God describes a heavenly city gathered from all nations that keeps their diversities, the classic Christian account of the particular and the universal. Locke is seated because the report names his Letter Concerning Toleration and its claim that no faith should cost a person civil rights. Washington closes because his letter to the Newport synagogue is the founding statement of equal citizenship rather than toleration, which is what the patriarchs asked for. Left off: the Second Vatican Council's Dignitatis Humanae, named in the report, which is in copyright and would be paraphrased only. The Pope, the patriarchs, the archbishop and the Syrian authorities are context only.

opening.text: This week's subject: what does solidarity with one's own people demand, and how does it coexist with universal love of neighbor? The report gives one side as many Christians, who argue this is persecution that Western governments and media underplay; ancient communities that have prayed in Aramaic for two thousand years are vanishing, and protecting them should be a priority in foreign policy and aid. The other side is those, including the Pope's own emphasis on dialogue, who stress that Christians suffer alongside Muslim neighbors amid general lawlessness and war; framing it as a clash of religions can feed sectarianism, and the path forward is the rule of law and peace for all. The patriarchs themselves asked for equal citizenship rather than special status. Begin.

turn.text: I wrote to a Roman governor who was torturing Christians, and I did not ask him for privileges. Not that Christians be favored, but that no one be kidnapped, ransomed or beaten for worshipping as he believes.

sittings.why_these_chairs: Augustine speaks first because the report names his City of God as one of the main texts on both sides, and because no Christian thinker has written more on the two cities. Calvin follows because the report names the two-kingdoms doctrine, and his Institutes gives the Reformed account of two governments with a magistrate charged to support true worship. Leo XIII is seated because the report names his Immortale Dei as the modern charter of Christendom, which also insists no one be forced into the faith. Roger Williams is seated because the report names his wall of separation, from the free-church side. Madison closes because his Memorial and Remonstrance is the founding American argument against even a small religious establishment. Left off: Luther, also named in the report, whose treatise on temporal authority was not among the verified texts this week; Calvin represents the Reformation's two-kingdoms view. The activists, Putin, Hegseth, Wilson and the Pope are context only.

opening.text: This week's subject: what is the proper relation between the City of God and the City of Man? The report gives one side as supporters, who say every government legislates someone's morality, and a nation formed by Christianity should openly govern by Christian principles rather than a neutral secularism that is itself a creed; believers have a duty to seek the good of the city through politics. The other side is critics, many of them Christians, who argue it confuses the two kingdoms, corrupts the church's witness by tying it to power, and misunderstands faith, which cannot be coerced: nations are not saved, people are, and religious liberty protects churches best when government stays out of theology. The same week a Russian president claimed his nation as the faith's ark. Both sides cite the Lord's words: “Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's.” (Matthew 22:21) and “My kingdom is not of this world” (John 18:36) Augustine, the two cities are yours. sittings.headline: Pope Leo XIV warns that ungoverned technology poses enormous risks and calls for keeping space peaceful
sittings.question: Is human mastery of nature a gift to be used or a power to be restrained, and who sets the limits? What is the human person for, and should machines do what makes us human?

setup.text: Reported on Nov 21, after a week in which the U.S. Catholic bishops opened their Baltimore assembly with a new task force on human dignity in the age of AI (Nov 16) and urged legal guardrails for transparency, accountability, human oversight and workers displaced by automation (Nov 18). sittings.why_these_chairs: Aristotle speaks first because the report names his living tools, the passage in the Politics that first imagined instruments working by themselves, and because his Ethics asks what every art is for. Bacon follows because the report names his New Atlantis and the Enlightenment confidence that knowledge relieves human suffering; his Advancement of Learning states that aim in his own words. Leo XIII is seated because the report names Rerum Novarum, the Church's first great teaching on work under new machines. Kant closes because the report names the danger of treating persons as means, which is his formula of humanity. Left off: Hans Jonas, Hayek and C.S. Lewis, named in the reports, who are in copyright, and Mary Shelley, whose Frankenstein is a novel rather than an argument. The Pope, the bishops, the Pentagon and the companies are context only.

opening.text: This week's subject: is human mastery of nature a gift to be used or a power to be restrained, and who sets the limits? The report gives one side as those who say the Church has the moral standing to insist that power over AI, weapons and space serve human dignity; without ethical limits and political rules, technology concentrates power and invites catastrophe, and a voice above markets and nations is needed. The other side is skeptics, who say calls for governance can slow innovation and hand control to bureaucracies or rival powers who will not comply, that frontiers have historically been opened by bold exploration rather than committees, and some question whether clergy should weigh in on technical policy. Both sides read the same charge in Genesis: “let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air, and over the cattle, and over all the earth” (Genesis 1:26) Aristotle, you imagined machines first. closing.text: Where they agreed: technology is good when it serves persons and wrong when it masters them. Where they split: Aristotle asks what the art is for and who it makes servants. Bacon defends discovery for the relief of human suffering while warning against learning sought for domination. Leo XIII names the displaced worker and a dignity no technology may outrage. Kant asks every rule to keep a responsible person wherever persons are affected.

I would not have clergy draft technical rules. But the Church has a duty to name the end every rule must serve, and to insist that public authority protect those whom progress leaves behind.

turn.text: Leo grounds dignity in God; I grounded it in reason, and we arrive at the same limit. “So act as to treat humanity, whether in thine own person or in that of any other, in every case as an end withal, never as means only.” (Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysic of Morals, Second Section) A machine is a means, and there is nothing wrong with using means. The wrong begins when persons are used merely as means, when a system manipulates a user, or decides who lives and dies in war, without anyone answerable for treating a person as an end.
